transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Hi Coleman, how are you?

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: Good, thanks.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: I wanted to have a chat with you because our friend Josh told me that you've joined a guitar group and it sounds interesting. I'd really like to learn myself.

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: Why don't you come along? I'm sure there's room for another person.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Really? So – who runs the classes?

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: He's called a 'coordinator' – his name's Gary <q id="1">Mathieson</q>.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Let me note that down. Gary. . . . How do you spell his surname?

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: It's M-A-T-H-I-E-S-O-N.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Right, thanks.

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: He's retired, actually, but he's a really nice guy and he used to play in a lot of bands.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Thanks. So how long have you been going?

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: About a month now.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: And could you play anything before you started?

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: I knew a few chords, but that's all.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: I'm sure everyone will be better than me.

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: That's what I thought, too. When I first spoke to Gary on the phone, he said it was a class for <q id="2">beginners</q>, but I was still worried that everyone would be better than me, but we were all equally hopeless!

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Oh, that's reassuring. So where do you meet?

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: Well, when I joined the group, they were meeting in Gary's home, but as the group got bigger, he decided to book a room at the <q id="3">college</q> in town. I prefer going there.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: I know that place. I used to go to tap dancing classes there when I was at secondary school. I haven't been since, though and I can't remember what road it's in . . . is it Lock Street?

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: It's just beyond there at the bottom of <q id="4">New</q> Street near the city roundabout.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Yes, of course.

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: The guitar club is on the first floor in Room T347.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Right. And when do you meet? Is it at the weekend?

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: We meet on Thursdays. It used to be 10.30 and that suited me well, but now we meet at <q id="5">11</q>. The class that's in there before us asked if they could have the room for another 30 minutes.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Oh, I see. Well, I'd love to come, but I don't have a guitar.

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: Well, you can always buy a second-hand one. There's a website called 'The perfect <q id="6">instrument</q>' that sells all kinds of guitars, violins and so on. I'm sure you'll find something there.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: So what's a typical lesson like with Gary?

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: Well, he always starts by getting us to tune our guitars. That takes about five minutes.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Uhuh.

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: Some people have an app they use, but others do it by <q id="7">ear</q>. Gary goes round and helps them. And while he's doing that, he tells us what he's going to do during the lesson.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: First, we usually spend about ten minutes doing some strumming.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: So is that using . . . what are they called . . . plectrums?

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: No – we just use our thumbs.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Much easier.

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: Gary reminds us where to put our fingers for each chord and then we play them together. Sometimes we all just start laughing because we're so bad at keeping time, so Gary starts <q id="8">clapping</q> to help us.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Do you learn to play any songs?

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: Yes – we do at least one song with words and chords. I mean that's harder than you think.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Oh, I'm sure it is!

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: That part of the lesson takes about 15 minutes. He often brings a <q id="9">recording</q> of the song and plays it to us first. Then he hands out the song and if there's a new chord in it, we practise that before we play it together – but really slowly.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Do you do any finger picking?

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: That's the last ten minutes of the lesson, when we pick out the individual notes from a tune he's made up. It's always quite simple.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: That must be hard, though.

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: It is, but people like it because they can really concentrate and if we're all playing well, it sounds quite impressive. The only trouble is that he sometimes gets us to play one at a time – you know, <q id="10">alone</q>.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: That's scary.

transcript.speaker: COLEMAN
transcript.text: It is, but I've got used to it now. At the end he spends about five minutes telling us what to practise for the following week.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Well, thanks Coleman. I'll go and have a look at that website, I think.

I never really planned to be a lifeboat volunteer when I came to live in Northsea. I'd been working in London as a website designer, but although that was interesting, I didn't like city life. <q id="11">I'd been really keen on boats as a teenager, and I thought if I went to live by the sea, I might be able to pursue that interest a bit more in my free time</q>. Then I found that the Lifeboat Institution was looking for volunteers, so I decided to apply.

The Lifeboat Institution building here in Northsea's hard to miss, it's one of the largest in the country. It was built 15 years ago with <q id="12">funds provided by a generous member of the public who'd lived here all her life</q>. As the Lifeboat Institution is a charity that relies on that kind of donation, rather than funding provided by the government, that was a huge help to us.

When I applied, I had to have a health assessment. The doctors were particularly interested in my vision. I used to be short-sighted, so I'd had to wear glasses, but I'd had laser eye surgery two years earlier so that was OK. <q id="13">They gave me tests for colour blindness and they thought I might have a problem there</q>, but it turned out I was OK.

When the coastguard gets an alert, all the volunteers are contacted and rush to the lifeboat station. Our target's to get there in five minutes, then <q id="14">we try to get the boat off the dock and out to sea in another six to eight minutes</q>. Our team's proud that we usually achieve that – the average time across the country's eight and a half minutes.

I've recently qualified as what's called a 'helmsman', which means I have the ultimate responsibility for the lifeboat. I have to check that the equipment we use is in working order – the crew have special life jackets that can support up to four people in the water. And <q id="15">it's ultimately my decision whether it's safe to launch the boat</q>. But it's very rare not to launch it, even in the worst weather.

As well as going out on the lifeboat, my work involves other things too. A lot of people underestimate how quickly conditions can change at sea, so <q id="16">I speak to youth groups and sailing clubs in the area about the sorts of problems that sailors and swimmers can have</q> if the weather suddenly gets bad. We also have a lot of volunteers who organise activities to raise money for us, and we couldn't manage without them.

The training we get is a continuous process, focusing on technical competence and safe handling techniques, and <q id="17">it's given me the confidence to deal with extreme situations without panicking</q>. I was glad I'd done a first aid course before I started, as that's a big help with the casualty care activities we do. We've done a lot on how to deal with ropes and tie knots – that's an essential skill. After a year, I did a one-week residential course, led by specialists. They had a wave-tank where they could create extreme weather conditions – so <q id="18">we could get experience at what to do if the boat turned over in a storm at night, for example</q>.
Since I started, I've had to deal with a range of emergency situations.

But the work's hugely motivating. It's not just about saving lives – I've learned a lot about the technology involved. My background in IT's been useful here, and I can use my expertise to help other volunteers. <q id="19">They're a great group – we're like a family really</q>, which helps when you're dragging yourself out of bed on a cold stormy night. But actually, <q id="20">it's the colder months that can be the most rewarding time</q>. That's when the incidents tend to be more serious, and you realise that you can make a huge difference to the outcome.
So if any of you listeners are interested. . . .

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: Hi Don – did you get the copy of the article on recycling footwear that I emailed you?

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: Yeah – it's here . . . I've had a look at it.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: So do you think it's a good topic for our presentation?

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: Well, before I started reading it, I thought recycling footwear, well, although it's quite interesting, <q id="21">perhaps there isn't enough to say about it</q>, cos we put shoes in recycling bins, they go to charity shops and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: . . . but there's much more to it than that.

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: I realise that now and I'm keen to research the topic more.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: That's great.

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: One of the things I didn't realise until I read the article was just how many pairs of trainers get recycled!

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: Well, a lot of young people wear them all the time now. They've become more popular than ordinary shoes.

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: I know. I guess they are very hard-wearing, but <q id="22">don't they look a bit casual for school uniform? I don't think they're right for that</q>.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: <q id="22">Actually, I think some of them look quite smart on pupils</q> . . . better than a scruffy old pair of shoes.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: So do you keep shoes a long time?

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: Yes. Though I do tend to wear my old pairs for doing dirty jobs like cleaning my bike.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: I must admit, I've <q id="23">recycled some perfectly good shoes, that haven't gone out of fashion and still fit, just because they don't look great on me any more</q>. That's awful isn't it?

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: I think it's common because there's so much choice. The article did say that recent sales of footwear have increased enormously.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: That didn't surprise me.

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: No. But then it said that <q id="24">the amount of recycled footwear has fallen: it's 6 percent now compared to a previous level of 11 percent. That doesn't seem to make sense</q>.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: That's because not everything goes through the recycling process. Some footwear just isn't good enough to re-sell, for one reason or another, and gets rejected.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: So let's find some examples in the article of footwear that was rejected for recycling.

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: OK. I think there are some in the interview with the recycling manager. Yeah – here it is.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: Mmm. Let's start with the ladies' high-heeled shoes. What did he say about those?

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: He said they were probably expensive – the material was suede and they were beige in colour – it looked like someone had only worn them once, but in a very wet field so <q id="25">the heels were too stained with mud and grass to re-sell them</q>.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: OK . . . and the leather ankle boots. What was wrong with them?

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: Apparently, the heels were worn – but that wasn't the problem. <q id="26">One of the shoes was a much lighter shade than the other one</q> – it had obviously been left in the sun. I suppose even second-hand shoes should look the same!

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: Sure. Then there were the red baby shoes.

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: Oh yes – we're told to tie shoes together when we put them in a recycling bin, but people often don't bother.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: <q id="27">You'd think it would have been easy to find the other, but it wasn't</q>. That was a shame because they were obviously new.

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: The trainers were interesting. He said they looked like they'd been worn by a marathon runner.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: Yeah – weren't they split?

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: Not exactly. <q id="28">One of the soles was so worn under the foot that you could put your finger through it</q>.

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: Well, we could certainly use some of those examples in our presentation to explain why 90 percent of shoes that people take to recycling centres or bins get thrown into landfill.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: Mmm. What did you think about the project his team set up to avoid this by making new shoes out of the good parts of old shoes?

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: It sounded like a good idea. They get so many shoes, they should be able to match parts. I wasn't surprised that it failed, though. I mean who wants to buy second-hand shoes really? Think of all the germs you could catch!

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: Well, people didn't refuse them for that reason, did they? <q id="29">It was because the pairs of shoes weren't identical</q>.

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: They still managed to ship them overseas, though.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: That's another area we need to discuss.

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: You know I used to consider this topic just from my own perspective, by thinking about my own recycling behaviour without looking at the bigger picture. So much happens once shoes leave the recycling area.

transcript.speaker: BELLA
transcript.text: It's not as simple as you first think, and <q id="30">we can show that by taking a very different approach to it</q>.

transcript.speaker: DON
transcript.text: Absolutely. So let's discuss . . .

For my project on invertebrates, I chose to study tardigrades. These are microscopic – or to be more precise – near-microscopic animals. There are well over a thousand known species of these tiny animals, which belong to the phylum Tardigrada. Most tardigrades range in length from 0.05 to 1 millimetre, though the largest species can grow to be 1.2 millimetres in length. They are also sometimes called 'water bears': 'water' because that's where they thrive best, and 'bear' <q id="31">because of the way they move</q>. 'Moss piglet' is another name for tardigrades because of the way they look when viewed from the front. They were first discovered in Germany in 1773 by Johann Goeze, who coined the name Tardigrada.

As I say, there are many different species of tardigrade – too many to describe here – but, generally speaking, the different species share similar physical traits. <q id="32">They have a body which is short</q>, and also rounded – a bit like a barrel – and the body comprises four segments. Each segment has a pair of legs, at the end of which are between four and eight sharp claws. I should also say that some species don't have any claws; <q id="33">what they have are discs</q>, and these work by means of suction. They enable the tardigrade to cling on to surfaces or to grip its prey. Within the body, there are no lungs, or any organs for breathing at all. Instead, <q id="34">oxygen and also blood are transported in a fluid that fills the cavity of the body</q>.

As far as the tardigrade's head is concerned, the best way I can describe this is that it looks rather strange – a bit squashed even – though many of the websites I looked at described its appearance as cute, which isn't exactly very scientific. <q id="35">The tardigrade's mouth is a kind of tube</q> that can open outwards to reveal teeth-like structures known as 'stylets'. These are sharp enough to pierce plant or animal cells.

So, where are tardigrades found? Well, they live in every part of the world, in a variety of habitats: most commonly, on the bed of a lake, or on many kinds of plants or in very wet environments. There's been some interesting research which has found that tardigrades are capable of surviving radiation and very high pressure, and <q id="36">they're also able to withstand temperatures as cold as –200 degrees centigrade, or highs of more than 148 degrees centigrade</q>, which is incredibly hot.

It has been said that tardigrades could survive long after human beings have been wiped out, even in the event of an asteroid hitting the earth. If conditions become too extreme and tardigrades are at risk of drying out, they enter a state called cryptobiosis. They curl into a ball, called a tun – that's T-U-N – by retracting their head and legs, and their metabolism drops to less than one percent of normal levels. They can remain like this until they are re-introduced to water, when they will come back to life in a matter of a few hours. While in a state of cryptobiosis, <q id="37">tardigrades produce a protein that protects their DNA</q>. In 2016, scientists revived two tardigrades that had been tuns for more than 30 years. There was a report that, in 1948, a 120-year-old tun was revived, but this experiment has never been repeated. There are currently several <q id="38">tests taking place in space, to determine how long tardigrades might be able to survive there</q>. I believe the record so far is 10 days.

So, erm, moving on. In terms of their diet, tardigrades consume liquids in order to survive. Although they have teeth, they don't use these for chewing. <q id="39">They suck the juices from moss, or extract fluid from seaweed</q>, but some species prey on other tardigrades, from other species or within their own. I suppose this isn't surprising, given that tardigrades are mainly comprised of liquid and are coated with a type of gel.

Finally, I'd like to mention the conservation status of tardigrades. It is estimated that they have been in existence for approximately half a billion years and, in that time, they have survived five mass extinctions. So, it will probably come as no surprise to you, that <q id="40">tardigrades have not been evaluated by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and are not on any endangered list</q>. Some researchers have described them as thriving.
Does anyone have any questions they'd like to ask?
